title: Waterloo Park plan update and 2026 schedule
subtitle: Uptown two-tower development public meeting, advisory committee dissolved, invasive species question, and local business recognition.
overview: Council launched an update of the Waterloo Park plan, looking ahead to a vision for 2050. It released $143,000 in capital funding, transferred $57,000 from the existing park plan implementation project, and dissolved the Waterloo Park Advisory Committee because it had met its mandate {{vote:m3}}. Staff said they will return in the spring with an engagement summary, with a final report expected in spring 2027. Council also approved the 2026 Council meeting schedule {{vote:m4}}.

Council held an informal public meeting on a zoning by-law amendment for 167-171 King Street South. The application proposes two towers on a five-storey podium, with a relocated heritage house. No decision was made. Residents raised concerns about height, wind, noise, sunlight, privacy, parking and the lack of ground-level green space. Staff will review the comments and report back at a future formal public meeting.

Council met in closed session for about an hour and a half on labour relations and land matters. The minutes report no decisions from it. Councillors also asked staff for an update on how the City manages invasive species, and thanked staff for recent community events and park work.

decisions.detail: Council approved report COM2025-023 and launched the update of the Waterloo Park plan.
Council released $143,000 in 2025 capital funding and transferred $57,000 from the park plan implementation project to the update project.
Council dissolved the committee because it had met its mandate.
Council approved report CORP2025-035 and the 2026 Council meeting schedule.

debate: The outgoing advisory committee chair said the committee's mandate had expired. The chair suggested a broader, multi-layered approach to public input, such as project-specific groups, instead of one long-standing committee of up to ten members.

A resident who organizes community events in the park said small, community-led events fall between arts and culture, neighbourhoods and parks, and are treated like private picnics. The resident suggested a no-fee permit like Toronto's pilot and a shared equipment library like the neighbourhood grant program. A councillor said staff should look at both.

Residents near the King Street South site raised concerns about the height of the towers, wind, noise from balconies and service vehicles, loss of sunlight and privacy for a neighbouring building, parking pressure, and no green space at ground level. One suggested a single tower or a cascading design.

The developer's team said the towers conform to existing tower regulations. They said bike rooms in their other buildings sit largely empty, a shared parking model would be used, and the heritage house would be reused, possibly as a restaurant. The requested density was set to allow for more two- and three-bedroom units.

Councillors asked staff to clarify the relationship between the proposed zoning and Official Plan Amendment 58, which is still awaiting provincial approval. They asked for comparable setbacks nearby, and for the wind study appendices to be posted online. One councillor also pushed back on suggestions that high-rise apartments are unsuitable for families.
